meta.title: Thai General Elections
sources: Wikipedia: Siamese and Thai general election articles 1933-2026 (results tables and infoboxes)
Election Commission of Thailand figures as reported there

eras.label: The 1932 experiment
eras.blurb: Siam's 1932 revolution replaced absolute monarchy with a constitution, and the first House of Representatives split its seats exactly down the middle: half chosen by voters, half appointed by the government, meant as a bridge to full representative rule. It held for four elections, 1933 to 1946, while the country renamed itself Thailand along the way.

eras.label: Coup, and half-appointed houses
eras.blurb: A 1947 coup abolished the parliament elected the year before and installed a new bicameral system, still with a large appointed bloc alongside the elected seats. Turnout in the February 1957 election jumped to 57%, which the source itself calls an indicator of heavy fraud, and Sarit Thanarat's own coup that September forced a rerun that December, the last vote before twelve years without an election.

eras.label: The generals' interlude
eras.blurb: Sarit and then Thanom Kittikachorn governed without a parliament for twelve years. When an election finally returned in 1969, it was the first in which every seat was elected rather than appointed, though 72 of 219 went to independents; the House was dissolved again within two years and Thailand went another six years without a vote.

eras.label: A crowded field, twice
eras.blurb: Elections in January 1975 and again in April 1976, after the House was dissolved early, both returned fractured parliaments of a dozen or more parties and short-lived coalitions. A coup in October 1976 shut elections down again, this time for three years.

eras.label: The Prem years
eras.blurb: Prem Tinsulanonda governed as an unelected prime minister through elections in 1979, 1983 and 1986 before Chatichai Choonhavan became the first elected prime minister in over a decade in 1988. A coup by the National Peace Keeping Council removed him in February 1991.

eras.label: Black May, and its rerun
eras.blurb: The March 1992 election handed power to Suchinda Kraprayoon, the coup leader turned unelected prime minister, and his appointment triggered the Black May protests that forced his resignation within weeks. A caretaker government called a fresh election that September, and two more followed in 1995 and 1996 as coalitions rose and fell within a few years of each other.

eras.label: Thaksin, and a coup
eras.blurb: The 1997 constitution gave Thailand its first 500-seat House with party-list seats alongside constituency ones. Thaksin Shinawatra's Thai Rak Thai won comfortably in 2001 and by landslide in 2005, then won a boycotted, nearly single-party rerun in 2006 that the Constitutional Court annulled months later, shortly before a September coup removed him from power outright.

eras.label: Two constitutions, two coups
eras.blurb: A junta-drafted constitution produced the 2007 election, won by a party aligned with the ousted Thaksin, and his sister Yingluck Shinawatra won again in 2011. Her snap election for February 2014 was blocked by opposition protesters occupying polling stations in parts of the country, voided by the Constitutional Court for not being held on a single nationwide day, and never rerun: a May 2014 coup ended the attempt.

eras.label: The junta's constitution
eras.blurb: The 2017 constitution, drafted under the military government that took power in 2014, let an entirely junta-appointed Senate join the House in choosing the prime minister, and did so in both 2019 and 2023 regardless of which party had actually won the most seats or votes. That provision expired before the 2026 election, the first since 2011 whose result determined the government on its own.

elections.label: December 1957
elections.summary: Independents finished first with 59 of 281 seats. Turnout 44.1%.
elections.caveat: Roughly half the House was still appointed rather than elected, a holdover from the 1932 constitution's transitional design.

elections.label: February 1957
elections.summary: Seri Manangkhasila Party finished first with 86 of 283 seats. Turnout 57.5%.
elections.caveat: Turnout of 57%, far above any earlier election, is described by the source as an indicator of heavy fraud, and 123 of the 283 seats still went to appointees rather than a vote.

elections.label: March 1992
elections.summary: Justice Unity Party finished first with 79 of 360 seats on 19.3% of the vote. Turnout 59.2%. Suchinda Kraprayoon replaced Anand Panyarachun.

elections.label: September 1992
elections.summary: Democrat Party finished first with 79 of 360 seats on 21.0% of the vote. Turnout 61.6%. Chuan Leekpai replaced Anand Panyarachun.
Thai Nation Party finished first with 92 of 391 seats on 22.8% of the vote. Turnout 62.0%. Banharn Silpa-archa replaced Chuan Leekpai.
New Aspiration Party finished first with 125 of 393 seats on 29.1% of the vote. Turnout 62.4%. Chavalit Yongchaiyudh replaced Banharn Silpa-archa.
Thai Rak Thai finished first with 248 of 500 seats. Turnout 69.4%. Thaksin Shinawatra replaced Chuan Leekpai.
Thai Rak Thai Party finished first with 377 of 500 seats on 60.5% of the vote. Turnout 72.6%. Thaksin Shinawatra stayed in office.
Thai Rak Thai finished first with 461 of 500 seats. Turnout 64.8%.
elections.caveat: The main opposition boycotted after a rule requiring even an unopposed candidate to clear 20% of the registered vote, leaving 39 seats vacant, and the Constitutional Court annulled the whole result months later.

elections.summary: People's Power finished first with 233 of 480 seats. Turnout 72.4%. Samak Sundaravej replaced Surayud Chulanont.
Pheu Thai Party finished first with 265 of 500 seats on 47.0% of the vote. Turnout 75.0%. Yingluck Shinawatra replaced Abhisit Vejjajiva.
Turnout 47.7%.
elections.caveat: Opposition protesters blocked candidate registration and polling in parts of the south, the Constitutional Court voided the result for not being held on a single nationwide day, and a May coup ended the attempt to rerun it before any seat was filled.

elections.summary: Pheu Thai Party finished first with 136 of 500 seats on 21.9% of the vote. Turnout 74.7%. Prayut Chan-o-cha stayed in office.
elections.caveat: The 250-seat Senate that would help choose the prime minister was appointed entirely by the outgoing junta and constituency boundaries were redrawn shortly before polling, an arrangement widely described at the time as a skewed race.

elections.summary: Move Forward Party finished first with 151 of 500 seats on 38.0% of the vote. Turnout 75.6%. Srettha Thavisin replaced Prayut Chan-o-cha.
